     6  module

    15  /-!
    16  # Semisimple linear endomorphisms
    17  
    18  Given an `R`-module `M` together with an `R`-linear endomorphism `f : M → M`, the following two
    19  conditions are equivalent:
    20  1. Every `f`-invariant submodule of `M` has an `f`-invariant complement.
    21  2. `M` is a semisimple `R[X]`-module, where the action of the polynomial ring is induced by `f`.
    22  
    23  A linear endomorphism `f` satisfying these equivalent conditions is known as a *semisimple*
    24  endomorphism. We provide basic definitions and results about such endomorphisms in this file.
    25  
    26  ## Main definitions / results:
    27  * `Module.End.IsSemisimple`: the definition that a linear endomorphism is semisimple
    28  * `Module.End.isSemisimple_iff`: the characterisation of semisimplicity in terms of invariant

    18  # Eigenvectors and eigenvalues
    19  
    20  This file defines eigenspaces, eigenvalues, and eigenvectors, as well as their generalized
    21  counterparts. We follow Axler's approach [axler2024] because it allows us to derive many properties
    22  without choosing a basis and without using matrices.
    23  
    24  An eigenspace of a linear map `f` for a scalar `μ` is the kernel of the map `(f - μ • id)`. The
    25  nonzero elements of an eigenspace are eigenvectors `x`. They have the property `f x = μ • x`. If
    26  there are eigenvectors for a scalar `μ`, the scalar `μ` is called an eigenvalue.
    27  
    28  There is no consensus in the literature whether `0` is an eigenvector. Our definition of
    29  `HasEigenvector` permits only nonzero vectors. For an eigenvector `x` that may also be `0`, we
    30  write `x ∈ f.eigenspace μ`.
    31  
    32  A generalized eigenspace of a linear map `f` for a natural number `k` and a scalar `μ` is the kernel
    33  of the map `(f - μ • id) ^ k`. The nonzero elements of a generalized eigenspace are generalized
    34  eigenvectors `x`. If there are generalized eigenvectors for a natural number `k` and a scalar `μ`,
    35  the scalar `μ` is called a generalized eigenvalue.
    36  
    37  The fact that the eigenvalues are the roots of the minimal polynomial is proved in
    38  `LinearAlgebra.Eigenspace.Minpoly`.
    39  
    40  The existence of eigenvalues over an algebraically closed field
    41  (and the fact that the generalized eigenspaces then span) is deferred to
    42  `LinearAlgebra.Eigenspace.IsAlgClosed`.
    43
